catalog_quote: Closed syllables are infrequent, under 1% of the total. The final consonant in CVC syllables is always a nasal, and the only consonant clusters in the language involve these syllable-final nasals. 1.3 Stress Stress does not carry contrastive meaning. The penultimate vowel in a word is stressed, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels. The exception occurs with word-final CVC syllables in which the ultimate vowel carries the stress; there is evidence which suggests that in these cases there is an underlying word-final /i/ or /u/ which has been dropped. When suffixing occurs, the stress transfers to the penultimate vowel in the suffixed form. In a word-final sequence of two vowels, if the first vowel is higher than the second, then the sequence consists of two syllables; otherwise, the sequence results in a single syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Gapapaiwa (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an empty rule field and no existing stress statements; this source supplies the placement (penultimate, non-contrastive, with alternating secondary stress and a final-CVC exception), so it refines rather than agrees or contradicts. new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress on the penultimate vowel (syllable) of the word; stress is recomputed on the suffixed word, so it stays penultimate under suffixation. The only exception is a word-final CVC syllable (final consonant always a nasal), which takes final stress; the author attributes this to a dropped underlying final /i/ or /u/, i.e. the stress is penultimate on the underlying form. Vowel sequences count as two syllables only when the first vowel is higher than the second; otherwise they form one syllable, which determines which vowel is 'penultimate'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels' (alternating, counted leftward from the primary penultimate stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final CVC syllables carry ultimate stress (explained as an underlying dropped final /i/ or /u/). On p. 310 the author also notes that the vowel-initial manner adverbs -ana 'continuously (plural subject)' and -ota 'just, only' are bound to the verb root 'as confirmed by morphophonemics and stress patterns', i.e. the stress domain is the verb plus these suffixes. The sketch is based on the Gapa dialect (Menapi village); the author states the two dialects Gapa and Paiwa differ only slightly (93% shared survey-list lexicon) and that 'the grammar is consistent throughout'.
new_statements.identity_note: McGuckin 2002 describes Gapapaiwa as spoken by about 3000 people on the south coast of the Cape Vogel peninsula, Milne Bay Province, with two dialects, Gapa (east) and Paiwa (west), divided by the Awitapu River; the author's data come from the Gapa dialect (Menapi village, fieldwork from April 1986) and she states the two dialects differ only slightly (93% identical survey-list lexicon; grammar consistent). Earlier mentions under the name Paiwa: Capell 1943, Lithgow 1976, Ross 1988. The stress statement is given for the language as a whole.

new_statements.relation_note: Same authors, same analysis as the catalog record (McGuckin 2002 sec. 1.3, classification weight): penultimate-vowel primary stress, alternating secondary stress to the left, final stress on word-final CVC syllables explained by a dropped final high vowel. Differences are wording only: 2008 hedges with 'overwhelmingly'/'usually', adds 'There is no contrastive tone or length in Gapapaiwa' and a word-final VV syllabification criterion, and omits the suffixation remark. Relative to the existing statement held by the project (read as 'fixed: penultimate syllable') it likewise agrees on placement; the CVC-final exception is what the catalog codes as weight.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the word; secondary stresses fall on alternate vowels leftward from it; words ending in a closed (CVC, coda /m n s/) syllable are the exception and take stress on the final vowel (the authors attribute this to a lost underlying final /i/ or /u/, which would make those forms regular penults underlyingly). Counting is by vowels, with word-final VV counted as two syllables only when the first vowel is higher than the second. No contrastive tone or length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'secondary stress usually occurs on alternating vowels preceeding it' (i.e. on every second vowel leftward from the stressed penultimate vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final CVC syllables carry stress on the ultimate vowel (evidence of an underlying dropped word-final /i/ or /u/); hedges 'overwhelmingly' (primary) and 'usually' (secondary) signal a residue of unexplained cases; CVC syllables are ~1% of syllables and their coda is restricted to /m/, /n/, /s/ (p. 7). The 2002 chapter's note on stress shifting to the new penult under suffixation is not repeated here.
new_statements.identity_note: Gapapaiwa [pwg], Oceanic (Papuan Tip cluster), north coast of Cape Vogel / Milne Bay Province, PNG; the OPD is by the same SIL team (Catherine and Ed McGuckin) whose 2002 Curzon sketch is the catalog source, so it describes the same variety.
